title: Book 11 — The visit to the dead
paragraphs: “When we reached the seashore, we dragged our ship into the water and loaded her mast and sails. We put the sheep aboard and took our places, weeping with heavy hearts. Circe, that great and cunning goddess, sent us a fair wind that blew steadily behind us, keeping our sails filled. We did whatever work the ship required and let her sail as the wind and helmsman directed. All day her sails stayed full as she held course across the sea, but when the sun set and darkness covered the earth, we entered the deep waters of the river Oceanus, where the land and city of the Cimmerians lie. They live wrapped in mist and darkness that the sun’s rays never pierce, neither when he rises nor when he sets again in the heavens. Those wretched people live in eternal, melancholy night. When we arrived there, we beached the ship, unloaded the sheep, and walked along the waters of Oceanus until we came to the place Circe had described.

“Here Perimedes and Eurylochus held the sacrificial animals while I drew my sword and dug a trench a cubit square. I made drink offerings to all the dead—first with honey and milk, then with wine, and finally with water. I sprinkled white barley meal over everything, praying earnestly to the helpless ghosts and promising them that when I returned to Ithaca, I would sacrifice my best barren heifer for them and load the funeral pyre with fine offerings. I especially promised Tiresias the finest black sheep from my flocks. When I had finished praying to the dead, I cut the throats of the two sheep and let their blood flow into the trench. Then the ghosts came streaming up from Erebus—young brides, unmarried men, old men worn out by toil, maidens who had been crossed in love, and brave warriors killed in battle with their armor still stained with blood. They came from every direction and flitted around the trench with a strange kind of screaming that made me pale with fear. When I saw them approaching, I ordered my men to quickly skin the dead sheep and burn them as offerings while reciting prayers to Hades and Persephone. But I sat with my drawn sword, refusing to let the helpless ghosts near the blood until Tiresias had answered my questions.

“The first ghost to appear was my companion Elpenor, for his body had not yet been buried. We had left him unwaked and unburied in Circe’s house because we had too much else to do. I was very sorry for him and wept when I saw him. ‘Elpenor,’ I said, ‘how did you get down here into this gloom and darkness? You reached this place on foot faster than I did with my ship.’

“‘Sir,’ he answered with a groan, ‘it was bad luck and my own terrible drunkenness. I was sleeping on the roof of Circe’s house and forgot to use the long staircase when I woke. I fell straight off the roof and broke my neck, so my soul came down to Hades’ realm. So I beg you, in the name of everyone you left behind—though they’re not here—your wife, the father who raised you as a child, and Telemachus, who is your house’s only hope: please do what I’m about to ask. I know that when you leave this underworld, you’ll sail your ship back to the Aeaean island. Don’t leave me there unwaked and unburied, or I might bring heaven’s anger upon you. Burn me with whatever armor I have, build a burial mound for me on the seashore that will tell future generations what an unlucky man I was, and plant over my grave the oar I used to row with when I was alive among my companions.’ And I replied, ‘My poor friend, I will do everything you’ve asked.’

“So we sat holding this sad conversation, I on one side of the trench with my sword held over the blood, and my comrade’s ghost speaking to me from the other side. Then came the ghost of my dead mother Anticlea, daughter of Autolycus. I had left her alive when I set out for Troy and was moved to tears when I saw her, but even in my grief, I wouldn’t let her approach the blood until I had questioned Tiresias.

“Then came the ghost of Theban Tiresias with his golden scepter in his hand. He recognized me and said, ‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, why, poor man, have you left the light of day and come down to visit the dead in this sorrowful place? Step back from the trench and put away your sword so I may drink the blood and give you true answers.’
“So I stepped back and sheathed my sword. When he had drunk the blood, he began his prophecy.

“‘You want to know about your homecoming,’ he said, ‘but heaven will make this difficult for you. I don’t think you’ll escape Poseidon’s notice—he still nurses his bitter grudge against you for blinding his son. Still, after much suffering, you may reach home if you can restrain yourself and your companions when your ship reaches the island of Thrinacia, where you’ll find the sheep and cattle belonging to the sun god, who sees and hears everything. If you leave these flocks unharmed and think only of getting home, you may yet reach Ithaca after much hardship. But if you harm them, I warn you of destruction for both your ship and your men. Even if you escape yourself, you’ll return in terrible condition after losing all your men, aboard another man’s ship, and you’ll find trouble in your house, which will be overrun by arrogant men who are consuming your wealth under the pretense of courting your wife and giving her presents.

“‘When you get home, you’ll take revenge on these suitors. After you’ve killed them by force or fraud in your own house, you must take a well-made oar and carry it on and on until you reach a country where people have never heard of the sea and don’t even salt their food, nor do they know anything about ships, or about oars, which serve as a ship’s wings. I’ll give you a sure sign you can’t miss: a traveler will meet you and say that what you carry on your shoulder must be a winnowing shovel. At this you must plant the oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Poseidon. Then go home and offer great sacrifices to all the heavenly gods, one after another. As for yourself, death will come to you from the sea, and your life will ebb away very gently when you’re full of years and at peace, and your people will bless you. All that I’ve said will come true.’

“‘This must be as heaven wills,’ I answered, ‘but tell me truly—I see my poor mother’s ghost nearby. She sits by the blood without saying a word, and though I’m her own son, she doesn’t recognize me or speak to me. Tell me, sir, how can I make her know me?’
“‘That I can easily explain,’ he said. ‘Any ghost you allow to taste the blood will speak to you rationally, but those you don’t give blood to will go away again.’

“At this, Tiresias’s ghost returned to Hades’ house, his prophecies complete. But I remained where I was until my mother came forward and tasted the blood. Then she recognized me at once and spoke lovingly, saying, ‘My son, how did you come down to this realm of darkness while still alive? It’s hard for the living to see these places, for between us and them lie great and terrible waters, and there is Oceanus, which no one can cross on foot—they must have a good ship to carry them. Have you been wandering all this time trying to find your way home from Troy? Haven’t you reached Ithaca yet or seen your wife in your own house?’

“‘Mother,’ I said, ‘I was forced to come here to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias. I’ve never yet come near the Achaean land or set foot in my native country. I’ve had nothing but one long series of misfortunes from the very first day I sailed with Agamemnon to Ilius, land of noble horses, to fight the Trojans. But tell me truly, how did you die? Did you have a long illness, or did heaven grant you a gentle, easy passage to eternity? Tell me also about my father and the son I left behind—is my property still in their hands, or has someone else seized it, thinking I won’t return to claim it? Tell me what my wife intends to do and what she’s thinking. Does she stay with my son and guard my estate safely, or has she made the best match she could and married again?’

“My mother answered, ‘Your wife remains in your house, but she’s in great distress and spends all her time weeping, both night and day. No one has yet taken possession of your fine property, and Telemachus still holds your lands undisturbed. He has to entertain a great deal, as of course he must, given his position as a magistrate, and everyone invites him out as well. Your father remains at his old place in the country and never goes near the town. He has no comfortable bed or bedding. In winter he sleeps on the floor by the fire with the servants and wears rags, but in summer, when warm weather returns, he lies outside in the vineyard on a bed of vine leaves scattered on the ground. He grieves constantly about your failure to return home and suffers more and more as he grows older. As for my own death, it happened this way: heaven didn’t take me swiftly and painlessly in my own house, nor was I struck by any illness that typically wears people down and kills them. Rather, my longing to know what you were doing and the force of my love for you—that’s what killed me.’

“Then I tried to find some way to embrace my poor mother’s ghost. Three times I sprang toward her and tried to clasp her in my arms, but each time she slipped from my embrace like a dream or phantom. Deeply hurt, I said to her, ‘Mother, why don’t you stay still when I try to embrace you? If we could put our arms around each other, we might find sad comfort in sharing our sorrows even here in Hades’ house. Does Persephone want to burden me with even more grief by mocking me with only a phantom?’

“‘My son,’ she answered, ‘most unfortunate of all mankind, Persephone isn’t deceiving you—this is simply how all people are when they’re dead. The sinews no longer hold flesh and bones together. These perish in the fierce heat of consuming fire as soon as life leaves the body, and the soul flits away like a dream. Now go back to the light of day as quickly as you can, and remember all these things so you can tell your wife later.’

“As we talked this way, Persephone sent up the ghosts of the wives and daughters of all the most famous men. They gathered in crowds around the blood, and I considered how I might question them individually. Finally I decided it would be best to draw the sharp blade from my sturdy thigh and prevent them all from drinking the blood at once. So they approached one by one, and each told me her lineage and family as I questioned her.

“The first I saw was Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, son of Aeolus. She fell in love with the river Enipeus, the most beautiful river in the whole world. Once when she was walking by its banks as usual, Poseidon, disguised as her beloved river, lay with her at the river’s mouth, and a huge blue wave arched itself like a mountain over them to hide both woman and god. Then he loosened her virgin belt and made her sleep deeply. When the god had completed his act of love, he took her hand and said, ‘Tyro, rejoice in good will—the embraces of gods are not fruitless, and around this time next year you’ll have fine twins. Take great care of them. I am Poseidon, so now go home, but keep silent and don’t tell anyone.’

“Then he dove under the sea, and in due time she bore Pelias and Neleus, both of whom served Zeus with all their might. Pelias became a great sheep breeder and lived in Iolcus, while the other lived in Pylos. Her other children were by Cretheus: Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon, who was a mighty warrior and charioteer.

“Next I saw Antiope, daughter of Asopus, who could boast of having slept in the arms of Zeus himself and bore him two sons, Amphion and Zethus. These founded seven-gated Thebes and built walls around it, for strong as they were, they couldn’t hold Thebes without fortifying it.
“Then I saw Alcmena, wife of Amphitryon, who also bore invincible Heracles to Zeus, and Megara, daughter of great King Creon, who married Amphitryon’s formidable son.

“I also saw fair Epicaste, mother of King Oedipodes, whose awful fate it was to marry her own son unknowingly. He married her after killing his father, but the gods revealed the whole story to the world. He remained king of Thebes in great grief for the gods’ spite against him, but Epicaste went to the house of the mighty jailer Hades, having hanged herself in her anguish, and the avenging spirits haunted him for his outraged mother—bringing him bitter regret thereafter.

“Then I saw Chloris, whom Neleus married for her beauty, giving priceless gifts for her. She was the youngest daughter of Amphion, son of Iasus and king of Minyan Orchomenus, and became queen of Pylos. She bore Nestor, Chromius, and Periclymenus, and also that marvelously lovely woman Pero, who was courted by all the surrounding country. But Neleus would only give her to whoever could steal Iphicles’ cattle from the grazing grounds of Phylace—a difficult task. The only man willing to attempt this cattle raid was a certain excellent seer, but heaven’s will was against him. The cattle guards captured and imprisoned him. Nevertheless, when a full year had passed and the same season came again, Iphicles freed him after he had interpreted all of heaven’s oracles. Thus Zeus’s will was accomplished.

“I saw Leda, wife of Tyndarus, who bore him two famous sons: Castor the horse-tamer and Polydeuces the mighty boxer. Both these heroes lie beneath the earth, though they’re still alive, for by Zeus’s special dispensation, they die and come back to life alternately, each living every other day throughout all time, and they have the rank of gods.

“After her I saw Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, who boasted of Poseidon’s embrace. She bore two sons, Otus and Ephialtes, but both were short-lived. They were the finest and best-looking children ever born in this world, except for Orion. At nine years old they were nine fathoms tall and nine cubits around the chest. They threatened to make war on the Olympian gods and tried to pile Mount Ossa on top of Mount Olympus, and Mount Pelion on top of Ossa, so they could scale heaven itself. They would have succeeded if they’d reached maturity, but Apollo, son of Leto, killed them both before they had even a trace of hair on their cheeks or chins.

“Then I saw Phaedra, Procris, and fair Ariadne, daughter of the magician Minos, whom Theseus was carrying off from Crete to Athens. But he didn’t enjoy her, for before he could, Artemis killed her on the island of Dia because of what Dionysus had said against her.

“I also saw Maera, Clymene, and hateful Eriphyle, who sold her own husband for gold. But it would take me all night to name every single wife and daughter of heroes I saw, and it’s time for me to sleep, either aboard ship with my crew or here. As for my escort home, heaven and you yourselves will arrange it.”
Here he finished, and all the guests sat enthralled and speechless throughout the covered gallery. Then Arete said to them:

“What do you think of this man, Phaeacians? Isn’t he tall and handsome, and isn’t he clever? True, he’s my guest, but all of you share in the honor. Don’t be hasty to send him away, and don’t be stingy with gifts to someone in such great need, for heaven has blessed all of you with great wealth.”

Then the aged hero Echeneus spoke, one of the oldest men among them: “My friends, what our noble queen has just said is both reasonable and appropriate, so be persuaded by it. But the final decision, whether in word or deed, rests with King Alcinous.”

“It will be done,” declared Alcinous, “as surely as I still live and rule the Phaeacians. Our guest is indeed eager to get home, but we must persuade him to stay with us until tomorrow, by which time I’ll be able to gather the full amount I intend to give him. His escort will be everyone’s concern, but especially mine as your chief.”

Odysseus answered, “King Alcinous, if you asked me to stay here for a full twelve months and then speed me on my way loaded with your noble gifts, I would gladly obey, and it would be greatly to my advantage, for I would return to my own people with fuller hands, and so be more respected and beloved by all who see me when I reach Ithaca.”

“Odysseus,” replied Alcinous, “none of us who see you think you’re a charlatan or swindler. I know many people go around telling such believable stories that it’s hard to see through them, but there’s a quality in your speech that assures me of your good character. Moreover, you’ve told the story of your own misfortunes and those of the Argives as skillfully as a practiced bard. But tell me truly, did you see any of the mighty heroes who went to Troy with you and died there? The evenings are still at their longest, and it’s not yet bedtime—continue with your divine story, for I could stay here listening until tomorrow morning, as long as you keep telling us of your adventures.”

“Alcinous,” answered Odysseus, “there’s a time for speeches and a time for sleep. Nevertheless, since you wish it, I won’t refrain from telling you the even sadder tale of those companions who didn’t fall fighting the Trojans but perished on their return through a wicked woman’s treachery.

“When Persephone had dismissed the female ghosts in all directions, the ghost of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, came sadly toward me, surrounded by those who had died with him in Aegisthus’s house. As soon as he tasted the blood, he recognized me and, weeping bitterly, stretched out his arms to embrace me. But he had no strength or substance anymore, and I too wept and pitied him. ‘How did you die, King Agamemnon?’ I asked. ‘Did Poseidon raise winds and waves against you at sea, or did your enemies kill you on land while you were stealing cattle or sheep, or while fighting to defend their wives and city?’

“‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes,’ he answered, ‘I wasn’t lost at sea in any storm Poseidon raised, nor did enemies kill me on the mainland. Aegisthus and my wicked wife murdered me together. He invited me to his house, feasted me, then butchered me as miserably as a fat beast in a slaughterhouse, while all around me my companions were slain like sheep or pigs for the wedding breakfast, or shared feast, or gorgeous banquet of some great lord. You must have seen many men killed in battle or single combat, but you never saw anything as truly pitiful as how we fell in that gallery, with the mixing-bowl and loaded tables lying about and the ground reeking with our blood. I heard Priam’s daughter Cassandra scream as my wife, Clytemnestra, killed her beside me. I lay dying on the ground with a sword in my body and raised my hands to kill the murderous slut, but she slipped away from me. She wouldn’t even close my lips or eyes as I died, for nothing in this world is as cruel and shameless as a woman who has fallen into such guilt as hers. Imagine murdering her own husband! I thought I’d be welcomed home by my children and servants, but her abominable crime has brought disgrace on herself and all women who come after—even the good ones.’

“‘Truly Zeus has hated the house of Atreus from first to last because of their women’s schemes,’ I said. ‘See how many of us died for Helen’s sake, and now it seems Clytemnestra plotted against you too during your absence.’

“‘Therefore be careful,’ continued Agamemnon, ‘and don’t be too trusting even with your own wife. Don’t tell her everything you know perfectly well. Tell her part of it and keep the rest to yourself. Not that your wife, Odysseus, is likely to murder you, for Penelope is a very admirable woman with an excellent character. We left her a young bride with an infant at her breast when we set out for Troy. That child is doubtless now grown to manhood, and he and his father will have a joyful meeting and embrace each other as they should, whereas my wicked wife didn’t even let me see my son before killing me. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—don’t announce your arrival when you bring your ship to Ithaca, but come secretly, for after all this, women can’t be trusted. But tell me truly, can you give me any news of my son Orestes? Is he in Orchomenus, or Pylos, or at Sparta with Menelaus? I assume he’s still living.’
“‘Agamemnon, why do you ask me?’ I said. ‘I don’t know whether your son is alive or dead, and it’s wrong to speak when one doesn’t know.’

“As we sat weeping and talking sadly together, the ghost of Achilles approached with Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and goodliest man of all the Danaans after Peleus’s son. Achilles, the fleet descendant of Aeacus, recognized me and spoke mournfully: ‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, what daring deed will you attempt next, that you venture down to Hades among us mindless dead, who are merely ghosts of those who can no longer work?’

“‘Achilles, son of Peleus, foremost champion of the Achaeans,’ I said, ‘I came to consult Tiresias to see if he could advise me about returning home to Ithaca, for I’ve never yet been able to reach the Achaean land or set foot in my own country, but have been in trouble constantly. As for you, Achilles, no one was ever as fortunate as you’ve been, nor ever will be, for all of us Argives adored you as long as you were alive, and now that you’re here, you’re a great prince among the dead. Don’t take it so hard that you’ve died.’

“‘Don’t speak to me of death’s consolations,’ he answered. ‘I’d rather be a hired laborer working for a poor man on earth than king of kings among the dead. But give me news about my son—has he gone to war and will he be a great soldier, or not? Tell me also if you’ve heard anything about my father Peleus—does he still rule among the Myrmidons, or do they show him no respect throughout Hellas and Phthia now that age has weakened his limbs? If I could stand beside him in the sunlight with the same strength I had when I killed the bravest of our foes on the plain of Troy—if I could be as I was then and go even briefly to my father’s house, anyone who tried to harm him or depose him would soon regret it.’

“‘I’ve heard nothing about Peleus,’ I answered, ‘but I can tell you all about your son Neoptolemus, for I brought him in my own ship from Scyros to join the Achaeans. In our war councils before Troy, he was always first to speak, and his judgment was flawless. Only Nestor and I could surpass him. When it came to fighting on Troy’s plain, he would never stay with the main body of troops but would dash far ahead, foremost of all in courage. He killed many men in battle—I can’t name every single one he slew while fighting for the Argives, but I’ll mention how he killed that brave hero Eurypylus, son of Telephus, the handsomest man I ever saw except Memnon. Many other Ceteians fell around him because a woman took bribes—his mother, bribed with gifts to send him to the war. Moreover, when all the bravest of the Argives climbed inside the horse Epeus had built, it fell to me to decide when we should spring our ambush or stay hidden. All the other leaders and chief men among the Danaans were wiping their eyes and trembling in every limb, but I never once saw him turn pale or brush a tear from his cheek. He kept urging me to break out from the horse, gripping his sword handle and bronze-tipped spear, breathing fury against the enemy. Yet when we had sacked Priam’s city, he received his handsome share of the prize money and boarded his ship (such is war’s fortune) without a wound, neither from a thrown spear nor in close combat, for the rage of Ares is a matter of great chance.’
“When I had told him this, Achilles’s ghost strode away across a meadow full of asphodel, rejoicing in what I’d said about his son’s prowess.

“The ghosts of other dead men stood near me, each telling his own sad story. But Ajax, son of Telamon, alone held back—still angry with me for winning our dispute over Achilles’s armor. Thetis had offered it as a prize, and the Trojan prisoners and Athena were the judges. I wish I had never won in such a contest, for it cost Ajax’s life—he who was greatest of all the Danaans after Peleus’s son in both stature and prowess.

“When I saw him, I tried to appease him, saying, ‘Ajax, won’t you forget and forgive even in death? Must the judgment about that cursed armor still anger you? It cost us Argives dearly to lose such a tower of strength as you were. We mourned you as much as we mourned Achilles, son of Peleus himself. The blame lies only with Zeus’s spite against the Danaans, for that’s what made him plan your destruction. Come here, master your proud spirit, and hear what I have to tell you.’

“He wouldn’t answer but turned away to Erebus and the other ghosts. Nevertheless, I would have made him speak despite his anger, or I would have gone on talking to him, except that there were still others among the dead I wanted to see.
“Then I saw Minos, son of Zeus, with his golden scepter, sitting in judgment on the dead. The ghosts were gathered sitting and standing around him in Hades’ spacious house, learning his verdicts.
“After him I saw huge Orion in a meadow full of asphodel, driving the ghosts of wild beasts he had killed in the mountains, holding a great bronze club in his hands, unbreakable forever.

“I saw Tityus, son of Gaia, stretched across the plain and covering about nine acres. Two vultures on either side were digging their beaks into his liver, and he kept trying to beat them off with his hands but couldn’t, for he had violated Zeus’s lover Leto as she traveled through Panopeus on her way to Pytho.

“I also saw Tantalus’s dreadful fate. He stood in a lake that reached his chin, dying of thirst but never able to reach the water. Whenever the poor wretch bent down to drink, it dried up and vanished, leaving nothing but parched ground—withered by heaven’s spite. Tall trees hung their fruit over his head—pears, pomegranates, apples, sweet figs, and juicy olives—but whenever the poor creature reached out to take some, the wind tossed the branches back up to the clouds.

“I saw Sisyphus at his endless task, pushing his enormous stone with both hands. With hands and feet he struggled to roll it up the hill, but always, just before he could push it over to the other side, its weight overcame him, and the pitiless stone would thunder back down to the plain. Then he would start trying to push it uphill again, sweat pouring off him and steam rising from his body.

“After him I saw mighty Heracles, but it was only his phantom, for he himself feasts eternally with the immortal gods and has lovely Hebe as his wife, daughter of Zeus and Hera. The ghosts were screaming around him like frightened birds flying in all directions. He looked black as night with his bare bow in his hands and an arrow on the string, glaring around as if always about to shoot. Around his chest was a wondrous golden belt decorated most marvelously with bears, wild boars, and lions with gleaming eyes. There was also war, battle, and death depicted on it. The craftsman who made that belt could never, no matter what he tried, make another like it. Heracles recognized me immediately and spoke sorrowfully: ‘Poor Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, are you too living the same miserable kind of life I lived when I was above ground? I was Zeus’s son, but I endured infinite suffering, for I became enslaved to someone far beneath me—a worthless man who set me all kinds of labors. He once sent me here to fetch the hell-hound, thinking he couldn’t find anything harder for me than this. But I brought the hound out of Hades and delivered him, for Hermes and Athena helped me.’

“At this, Heracles went back down into Hades’ house, but I stayed where I was in case some other mighty dead might come to me. I would have seen still others who are gone before, whom I longed to see—Theseus and Pirithous, glorious children of the gods—but so many thousands of ghosts gathered around me uttering such terrifying cries that I was struck with panic, fearing Persephone might send up from Hades’ house the head of that awful monster, the Gorgon. At this I hurried back to my ship and ordered my men to board immediately and cast off the mooring ropes. So they embarked and took their places, and the ship went down the stream of the river Oceanus. We had to row at first, but soon a fair wind sprang up.
